time_scope: native and Sino-Korean strata, Present Day Korean background
claim: Liquids are prohibited word-initially in native and Sino-Korean vocabulary; native words have no underlying initial liquid.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Normatively permitted exceptions include the letter name /LiɨL/ and some family names with original initial liquids; actual pronunciation may vary.

claim: Word-initial underlying Sino-Korean /L/ is realized as [n] or deleted; deletion occurs before [i] or [j] because initial [ni] and [nj] are themselves restricted.
normalized_environment: INITIAL_LIQUID repair: [n]; before HIGH_FRONT_VOCOID /i,j/: DELETE due to *#ni,*#nj
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Kang notes an alternative analysis in which these forms are lexicalized as n-initial or vowel-initial, so synchronic productivity of the alternation is disputed.

claim: Recent English loanwords relax the native initial-liquid restriction: both English /l/ and /ɹ/ are generally adapted as word-initial [ɾ].
normalized_environment: LOAN_STRATUM licenses WORD_INITIAL_LIQUID; English /l,ɹ/ neutralize to [ɾ] generally
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Actual loanword realization is variable and the native initial-avoidance rule remains marginally active; a separate record captures this rather than treating [ɾ] as categorical.

claim: English liquid contrasts are mapped differently by position: intervocalic /l/ is generally geminate [ll] while intervocalic /ɹ/ is singleton [ɾ]; coda /l/ surfaces [l], whereas English coda /ɹ/ is generally lost.
normalized_environment: INTERVOCALIC English l->LL, r->ɾ; CODA l->[l], English r->∅
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Medial /l/ shows substantial historical and speaker variation between singleton [ɾ] and geminate [ll]; the stated pattern is the Present Day generalization, not an exceptionless mapping.

time_scope: Enlightenment Period Korean 1890-1910; 1930s; Present Day Korean
claim: Written loanword data show increasing retention of initial liquids over time: 96.3% in Enlightenment Period Korean, 98.5% in the 1930s, and 100% in the Present Day Korean NIKL 1991 list.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Orthographic retention does not guarantee liquid pronunciation: spoken Present Day data still include nasal realizations.

time_scope: Choi 2001 pronunciation survey interpreted by Kang 2012
claim: Despite categorical initial-liquid spelling in the Present Day written corpus, spoken Seoul Korean still shows marginal application of initial-liquid avoidance, including [n] realizations; the process is therefore gradient and speaker-dependent rather than extinct.

source_forms.sample: Choi 2001: 12 liquid-initial loanwords produced by 367 Seoul speakers and 34 broadcasters
source_forms.reported_group_rates: [n] 3.5% in general Seoul speakers vs 2.3% in broadcasters; [l] 6.1% vs 9.2%, differences not statistically significant (p=0.2953)

normalized_environment: VARIABLE #LIQUID -> [n]/LIQUID in PDK; native avoidance MARGINALLY PRODUCTIVE
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The written NIKL list has 100% liquid transcription, so orthography and production distributions must be kept separate.
